Well, it’s... I guess it’s complicated. I mean, with teaching, I do still care about my students. I really do. Most days I can still put on that big teacher smile for them and get through the lessons, you know, especially when they’re excited about a project or they finally grasp a concept we've been working on all week. But... I don't know, it’s like, underneath all of that performance, there’s just this... this gray, flat feeling. It’s not like I'm crying all the time, it’s just this heavy dullness. And it just clings to me. It follows me right out the school doors, sits in the car with me, and follows me all the way home. 

And because of that, the things outside of work... well, I used to be so active with them. I have this garden with these raised beds I put in a couple of summers ago, and I used to do watercolors, too—mostly botanical stuff, painting the things I grew. I even have a little station set up for it with all my nice paints right by the window. But now... even my garden or my watercolors just seem so far away. Like, I can see the weeds that need pulling, or I look at my brushes, and I just feel completely disconnected from it all. I keep telling myself, 'Oh, I'll paint this weekend, it'll make me feel better,' but then Saturday comes and that flat feeling is just blanketing everything, and I can't even bring myself to open the sketchbook. It’s like the joy has just been drained out of the things that used to recharge me.

Sad... well, yeah, I suppose that's exactly what I was just trying to explain with that whole gray, flat feeling I mentioned a second ago. It’s funny you use the word sad, because I think a lot of people assume sadness means you’re just sobbing all day or, you know, watching tragic movies in bed with a box of tissues. I teach fourth grade, and you really have to be 'on' for them, so I get through the lessons, I do the silly voices when I read aloud, I cheer them on during math games. I can do all of that. But underneath all of that performance, that gray feeling is just anchoring me down. It’s a very quiet kind of sad. And it really does just follow me right out the door and all the way home. 

It’s exactly why the garden and the watercolors feel so distant, like I was just telling you. It’s like I’m looking at my own life through a foggy window. I'll be standing in my kitchen, looking out at the raised beds I built, or I'll walk past my painting desk, and I just feel this profound... well, this sadness that just coats everything. It makes it all seem so far away, even when it's right in front of me. So, yes, even though I'm functioning and smiling at work, that sad, flat feeling is pretty much always there, just humming in the background of my entire day, from the minute I wake up to the minute I go to sleep.

No... no, not really. It's like the part of my brain that used to light up when I did something enjoyable has just... gone dark.

I can't think of a single thing right now that actually brings me that feeling of pleasure or joy. It's just... all so flat.

Well, it’s... gosh, it feels like forever, to be honest. But if I really sit and trace it back, I’d say it’s been about two years and two months. I know that sounds oddly specific, but I can actually pinpoint it because it started right around the time my husband stopped working outside the home. 

He was a project manager at this mid-sized logistics firm—he’d been there for almost eight years, and he used to commute about forty-five minutes each way. So, you know, our mornings had this whole rhythm. We’d wake up, have coffee together, I’d head off to school, he’d head to the office. But then his company restructured, and he transitioned to being entirely remote, working from our spare bedroom. And I know it sounds like it shouldn't be a big deal—I mean, a lot of people work from home now, and it’s supposed to be this great, flexible thing. But it completely upended our household routine. 

Suddenly, he was just *always* there. And I love him, I really do, but when I’d come home from a long day of teaching fourth graders—which, as I mentioned, takes so much energy just to put on that happy face and be 'on' all day—I used to have this quiet house to come back to. I could decompress, maybe go out to the garden, or just sit in silence for an hour before he got home. But then, he was just always in the house, pacing around on conference calls, or wanting to chat the second I walked through the door because he’d been cooped up all day. 

And that’s when I first started noticing that heavy, gray feeling creeping in. At first, I just thought I was tired from the school year, or maybe just adjusting to the new dynamic. I kept telling myself, 'Give it a month, give it two months, you'll get used to his new schedule.' But the months just kept passing. We had our anniversary that fall, then the holidays, then another spring planting season came and went, and that flat, dull emptiness just never lifted. It just settled over me like a heavy blanket. So, yeah, it’s been over two years now... about two years and two months of just dragging myself through this fog every single day.

Well, gosh, I feel like I might be repeating myself a little bit here, but... yes, it’s exactly those things I was just telling you about a minute ago. The watercolors, the garden, the reading. Those were the things I used to enjoy so, so much.

It was my absolute favorite part of the week, just watching the pigment bleed into the wet paper. It was so peaceful. 

But now, like I was saying, the tin literally has a layer of dust on it. I walk past my painting desk in the spare room and I just feel guilty, honestly, because he spent good money on it and I can't even bring myself to open the lid.

But I had to drop out last year. I just couldn't get through the chapters anymore. I'd sit there on the couch, staring at the pages, and I'd realize I'd been looking at the exact same sentence for ten minutes without absorbing a single word. 

So, I'm sorry if I'm just saying the same things over again, but those are really the main ones. The painting, the gardening, the books, even those evening walks... they all used to bring me so much light and give me a break from the stress of teaching, and now they just feel like... I don't know, like heavy obligations that I just can't seem to meet.

No, not really. I mean, I've always been a pretty consistent person when it comes to those things, you know? My husband jokes that you could set a watch by my stomach and my bedtime.

Like I should be sleeping for fourteen hours a day or forgetting to eat because I'm so miserable. But no, my body is just chugging along on its usual schedule, completely ignoring the fact that my brain feels like it's trudging through wet cement. So, no, no significant changes at all in sleep or appetite. Just the same old routine.

They'd just tune me out or start talking over me. Well... it depends on how you define functioning, I guess. 

I mean, on a basic, baseline level? Yes, I'm functioning. I'm still getting up when my alarm goes off at 5:45 every morning. I'm still showing up for my students, getting through the math lessons, making sure the state standards are met. And I'm still showing up for my family, too. I make sure the house doesn't fall apart, I help my husband figure out dinner, I do the laundry. So, you know, the wheels haven't completely fallen off the bus. To the outside world, I probably look like I'm doing just fine.

But... if you look a little closer, or if you ask the people who really know me, yeah, it’s definitely interfering. Because I've just... I've pulled back from absolutely everything else. Everything that isn't strictly mandatory for survival. 

Like I was saying earlier about that mentoring opportunity with the new teacher... that’s a perfect example. I used to be the first one to volunteer for things like that. I loved being on committees, organizing the staff holiday party, really being part of the school community. Now I just keep my head down, do my job, and walk straight to my car the second the final bell rings. 

And socially, it's the exact same story. My husband and I used to have this group of friends we'd meet up with for trivia night at this little pub downtown every other Thursday. We’ve been doing it for years, and we even won the grand prize a couple of times—we had this whole running joke about our team name. But lately, I just... I can't bring myself to go. By the time Thursday evening rolls around, the thought of sitting in a noisy room and trying to be witty and conversational, pretending I have energy I don't have... it's just completely overwhelming. So I tell my husband to go without me, and I just stay home on the couch. I've turned down lunch dates with my girlfriends, weekend brunches... I just don't have it in me.

And it's even the little things at home, you know? The creative routines that used to keep my life feeling full and... I don't know, vibrant, I guess. I used to love watercolor painting. I have this whole beautiful setup in our spare bedroom, right by the window where the natural light is really good in the late afternoons. I used to come home from school, put on a podcast or some classical music, and just paint for an hour to decompress. It was my favorite part of the day. But I haven't touched my brushes in... gosh, it has to be months now. The water cups on the desk are completely bone dry, the paints are probably hardening in their tubes. I just walk past that room and close the door because looking at it makes me feel guilty. 

So, yes, I’m functioning in the sense that I’m doing my job and paying the bills, but all the color is kind of gone from it. I’m just doing the bare minimum to get by, and I've completely dropped all the parts that actually made it a fulfilling life.

Well, worsening... I don't know if I'd say it's getting *worse*, exactly. It's more like it's just... static? Significantly impacting my ability to enjoy life... honestly, I really don't think so. I mean, it goes right back to what I was just saying about the bakery and my students. The actual *ability* to feel joy or to enjoy a moment, that hasn't gone anywhere.
